evidenceAudit.scope: Primary health centre and school-health staff in Saudi Arabia measuring weight and height in children and adolescents aged 2 to 18 years, classifying weight status, screening for complications (blood pressure, blood glucose, lipids, liver enzymes, mental health), and referring to a multidisciplinary service. Uses the World Health Organization fact sheet, the Endocrine Society guideline abstract, an Obesity Medicine Association review and a 2026 Saudi primary care study. Not for drug or surgical treatment, which belongs to specialist services.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Health Council childhood obesity guideline was found; the Saudi study used the United States Centers for Disease Control body mass index percentile cut-offs (overweight 85th to below 95th, obesity 95th or above) and the World Health Organization uses standard deviation cut-offs, so the Saudi reference chart to be used in the clinic should be confirmed locally.

The full text of the Endocrine Society 2017 guideline and the American Academy of Pediatrics 2023 guideline could not be opened from this environment; only the Endocrine Society abstract was read, so its detailed recommendations (such as the order of comorbidity testing) are not written.
The screening ages and alanine aminotransferase thresholds come from a secondary review of the North American paediatric liver society guidance, not from the original guideline.
Blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipid and HbA1c thresholds for children were not found in the sources and are not written; use the national or international paediatric reference tables.
The World Health Organization fact sheet was read through an automated summary, so section headings are approximate; confirm the figures at source.

No medicine is written: the Endocrine Society abstract says weight-loss drugs in childhood and adolescence should be restricted to clinical trials, and newer paediatric obesity drug labels were not reviewed.
Figures were read by automated extraction of web and article text; spot-check each figure against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Obesity is a chronic disease from environmental, psychosocial and biological factors including genetic susceptibility (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Causes). Pediatric obesity has its basis in genetic susceptibilities influenced by a permissive environment starting in utero (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion). Endocrine causes of obesity are rare and usually come with attenuated growth (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion). In 28,275 Saudi children aged 2 to 14, obesity rose from 6.2% at ages 2 to 3 to 23.8% at ages 12 to 14 (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Results). Urbanisation, processed energy-dense food, sugary drinks and sedentary behaviour drive obesity in Saudi Arabia (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Discussion).

symptoms: Most children have no symptoms; weight gain is found at routine measurement (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Fatigue and vague abdominal discomfort can occur with fatty liver, which is often silent (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).
Low mood, bullying or poor self-esteem: the psychological toll of obesity needs mental health screening (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
physicalSigns: Weight-for-height above 3 standard deviations in children under 5, or body mass index-for-age above 2 standard deviations at 5 to 19 years (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Definitions).
Hypertension and other complications to be checked at assessment (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Slowed growth with obesity suggests an endocrine cause (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
redFlags: Obesity with attenuated growth, specific syndromic features or early severe onset: look for an endocrine or genetic cause (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Hypertension, abnormal glucose or lipids, or raised liver enzymes: assess and treat the complication (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Mental health symptoms: screen and provide counselling (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Severe obesity or pan-hypopituitarism: screen the liver earlier (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).
precipitants: Maternal obesity and excessive weight gain in pregnancy and the first two years of life (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Background).
Parental obesity, family history and socioeconomic factors (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Background).
Birth weight, gestational age and breastfeeding practices (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Background).
Ultra-processed food, sugary drinks, low physical activity and screen time (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Prevention).
Increasing age: obesity is nearly four times as common at 12 to 14 as at 2 to 3 years (Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Results).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Normal or tall stature and no syndromic features (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Slowed growth, for example hypothyroidism or Cushing syndrome (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Specific historical or physical features such as early severe onset (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Body mass index-for-age above 1 but not above 2 standard deviations at ages 5 to 19 (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Definitions).
High body mass index with a lean physique; assess clinically (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).

clinicalManagement.title: Measure and classify
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At routine well-child and school visits
actions: Measure weight and height and plot body mass index-for-age (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Classify weight status with the chart in use: above 1 standard deviation overweight, above 2 obesity at 5 to 19 years (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Definitions).
Use sensitive language and avoid blaming the child or family (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).

clinicalManagement.title: Take history and examine
actions: Ask about diet, sugary drinks, physical activity, sleep, screen time, family history and pregnancy and infancy history (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Prevention; Saudi child obesity prevalence study, Section Background).
Check growth pattern and syndromic features to find the rare endocrine or genetic cause (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Measure blood pressure and screen for mental health problems (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management; Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).

clinicalManagement.title: Screen for complications
actions: Send alanine aminotransferase from age 9 to 11 for obesity, or overweight with other risk factors, and earlier in severe obesity (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).
Add fasting glucose, HbA1c and a lipid profile (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).
Do not rely on a normal liver enzyme to exclude fatty liver (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel the family
actions: Give evidence-based advice on diet, physical activity and sleep to every family (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Prevention and healthy lifestyle come first, because lasting results are hard once obesity is established (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer for multimodal care
actions: Refer children with obesity to behavioural, nutritional and psychological support in a multimodal chronic care service (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Refer to a paediatric endocrinologist or geneticist if there are endocrine or syndromic features (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
Refer to a paediatric hepatologist for persistently raised alanine aminotransferase or a high-risk liver picture (Obesity Medicine Association paediatric liver review, Section Question 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Plan long-term follow-up
actions: Build an individual long-term care plan with regular follow-up and monitor response (WHO obesity fact sheet, Section Management).
Plan the transition to adult care for adolescents (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is written in this screening topic. The Endocrine Society guideline abstract states that weight-loss medicines in childhood and adolescence should be restricted to clinical trials, and that bariatric surgery is for the most seriously affected mature teenagers who have failed lifestyle modification, in experienced teams. Newer paediatric obesity medicine labels were not reviewed, so prescribing is for a paediatric specialist service and a current Saudi Food and Drug Authority register check.

learningObjectives: Measure weight and height and classify weight status at routine visits.
Screen for complications: blood pressure, glucose, lipids, liver enzymes and mood.
Counsel the whole family on diet, activity and sleep.
Refer to multimodal care and look for rare endocrine causes.
pitfalls: Missing growth failure that suggests an endocrine cause.
Offering advice to the child without the family.
keyPoints: Do not label or blame the child.
A normal liver enzyme does not exclude fatty liver.
Medicines and surgery are specialist decisions.

patientEducation: Weight is one part of a child's health. We measure it to help, not to blame.
Offer water instead of sugary drinks, regular meals at home and more family activity.
Limit screens and make sure your child sleeps well.
Obesity can affect blood pressure, sugar, liver and mood, so we check these.
Treatment is long term and works best as a family.
lifestyleAndDiet: Be active for most of the day with play, walking and sport.
Eat more vegetables, fruit, whole grains and legumes and fewer processed foods.
Eat meals together and limit snacking in front of screens.
mdtReferrals: Primary care doctor and nurse; school health nurse; dietitian; physiotherapist or exercise specialist; psychologist; paediatric endocrinologist; paediatric hepatologist.
dischargeCriteria: Not applicable as a discharge: record the weight status, screening done, family plan, referrals and next review date.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review weight, blood pressure and family plan at regular intervals; repeat laboratory screening as advised by the specialist; plan transition to adult care in adolescence (Endocrine Society paediatric obesity guideline, Section Conclusion).
